title: The Man Who Remembered Everyone
logline: An ordinary tired man misses a friend's mother's name at the worst possible moment, stops trying to remember his people, starts keeping them in plain files an agent can read, and eleven months later says the name before he is asked.

beats.text: My friend called on a Tuesday to tell me his mother had died.
beats.provenance: reality: the ordinary case that makes relationship memory matter. Gary Sheng's PRM practice exists because the cost of forgetting lands hardest at the moments you cannot prepare for.

beats.text: I said all the right things. I never said her name, because I did not know it. He had told me twice.
beats.provenance: reality: the specific failure mode of unaided relationship memory. Being told a fact twice and still not holding it is what a kept record fixes and willpower does not.

beats.text: That is what a conversation was for me. It happened, and it was real, and then it was gone.
beats.provenance: reality: the default state of every conversation before a capture practice exists.

beats.text: I was not careless about it. I had voice memos on my phone, notes in one app, a recorded call in another. None of them talked to each other, and I never opened any of them again.
beats.provenance: reality: the real precursor state of Gary Sheng's pipeline. Apple Voice Memos, Granola meeting notes, iMessage audio and call recordings each held real material in a separate silo, and the sync skills (sync-granola, parse-imessage-convo, auto-transcribe) exist because none of them read each other.

beats.text: So I stopped trying to remember. I kept it instead.
beats.provenance: the turn of the testimony. Reality: the decision to treat memory as a storage problem rather than a discipline problem.

beats.text: Every recording became a plain file with a plain name, in one folder, on my own machine. Nothing clever. Just kept.
beats.provenance: reality: garyinparadise is a pure-markdown knowledge base with no framework, roughly 770 relationship files and 700 transcript records, named by convention and stored locally. The plainness is the design.

beats.text: The folder was not the point. Being able to read every file in it at once was the point.
beats.provenance: reality: the load-bearing claim of the practice. A local corpus is only worth keeping because an agentic harness can read the whole of it per question.

beats.text: So I gave it to something that reads. It does not remember anything, and it never needs to. It reads the folder every time.
beats.provenance: reality: Claude Code over a local markdown corpus. The agent is stateless per question and re-reads the files, which is why the files rather than the model are the durable asset.

beats.text: What came back was a wall of small lights, one for each person I have, holding everything they ever told me.
beats.provenance: reality: the bidirectional relationship-to-transcript link that is the core architectural pattern of the corpus. Every transcript names its participants and every relationship file carries its own transcript table.

beats.text: Most of them were dark at first. I had twenty years of people and almost none of it kept.
beats.provenance: reality: the honest starting condition. A relationship corpus begins almost entirely empty, and the backlog before the practice is unrecoverable.

beats.text: It fills faster than you would think. A month of ordinary calls is a lot of light.
beats.provenance: reality: the observed fill rate of the practice. Ordinary weekly conversation volume compounds into a usable corpus within months, without any special effort.

beats.text: Eleven months later, the same friend called.
beats.provenance: reality: the payoff interval. The value of a kept record is realized at a distance long enough that unaided memory has certainly failed.

beats.text: Before I picked up, I knew what he was carrying, and I knew her name was Ruth.
beats.provenance: reality: PRM lookup before a call. The relationship file surfaces prior context, and the name is the smallest and most load-bearing fact in it.

beats.text: I said it first. He went quiet, and then he cried, and we talked for an hour about her.
beats.provenance: the testimony's resolution, and the answer to the wound in beat 2.

beats.text: People tell me this saves me hours every week. It does. That is the smallest thing it does.
beats.provenance: reality: the efficiency framing is true and is the weakest available reason to do it. The strong reason is the one in beat 14.

beats.text: I am not better at remembering than I was. I keep it, and I can find it, and so nobody I love has to be a stranger to me twice.
beats.provenance: the refrain resolved. Reality: the practice does not improve recall, it removes the dependence on recall.
